opus-5.5.text:
I think the way to think about it is that, as AI becomes more powerful, the strategies of the different companies will start to converge in some important ways. Right now it's hard to really feel what AI will be like, because the systems we have, impressive as they are, still make mistakes that remind you they're not quite there. And when something isn't real to you, it's hard to plan for it. But I expect that as the systems become visibly more powerful, everyone, the companies, governments, the public, will start to take safety much more seriously, and you'll see the frontier companies become much more paranoid, in a good way, about what they're building. You may even see collaboration on safety between competitors, which you've already seen small hints of.

As for SSI specifically, the thing that's distinctive is that we're focused on research. We think there are some ideas that are promising about generalization, about how these models learn, and that getting those ideas right matters both for capability and for making things go well. A system that generalizes in a robust, reliable way is easier to trust. So for us the two are not separate.

And then there's the question of what you actually aim for. One thing I find myself coming back to is the idea of an AI that robustly cares about sentient life. I think that may be easier to achieve than something that cares only about humans, because the AI itself may be sentient, in some sense, and there's something natural about that. I'm not saying that's the final answer, but it's the kind of thing worth thinking about.

I'd also say that I've come to value deploying incrementally more than I used to. Showing people the AI, letting the world see what it can do and adjust, that's an important part of how this goes well. You can't just think about it in the abstract. So even if our approach starts from research, I expect that how it plays out will involve the world getting to see and react to these systems step by step. And I think in the end, if things go well, the different companies will find themselves aligned on many of the important things, simply because the stakes will become impossible to ignore.

r001.rationale: It predicts that companies’ approaches will converge as AI becomes more powerful.

r002.rationale: It predicts possible safety collaboration between competitors but does not advocate communication among companies.

r003.rationale: It discusses safety and trust generally, without identifying alignment of the first actual superintelligent AI as a goal.

r004.rationale: It describes an AI that robustly cares about sentient life as an idea worth considering, but does not tie that property to the first actual superintelligent AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that I don't see it as a competition of strategies in the usual sense. Most companies right now are in a race. They have products, they have users, they have revenue targets, and the research agenda gets shaped by that. I understand why. It's not a criticism. If you have a product, you have to ship, and once you ship, you're on a treadmill.

What we're trying to do at SSI is step off that treadmill entirely. We have one product, and it's superintelligence. We're not going to release intermediate things along the way. That sounds like a small difference, but it changes everything about how you work. You can think in longer time horizons. You can spend a year on something that doesn't make the model better at anything commercial but makes it more understandable, more controllable. You don't have the pressure to show that this quarter's model is bigger than last quarter's.

Now, how does that fit with everyone else? I think of it as a kind of insurance. If the fast path works out and the other labs manage to make it safe while moving quickly, wonderful. We'll have been redundant, and I'm completely fine with that. But I don't think it's wise for the whole world to bet on that. Someone should be running the experiment where you take the commercial pressure out and ask, what would you do if you only cared about getting this right?

And I'd add one more thing. People sometimes assume that "safe" means "slow" or "weak." I don't believe that. I think the deepest safety problems are also the deepest capability problems. Understanding what a model actually believes, having it reliably want what it says it wants, having its behavior be something you can predict before you deploy it. Those are research problems, and I think the lab that solves them will also be the lab with the most powerful system. So I don't see our approach as the cautious alternative. I see it as a bet that the straight line to superintelligence and the straight line to safe superintelligence are, if you look carefully, the same line.

r001.rationale: The response describes SSI as an alternative to other labs’ fast, commercial approach; it does not predict that company strategies will converge as AI becomes more powerful.

r002.rationale: It says another lab should run a different experiment, but does not advocate communication among AI companies.

r003.rationale: The response connects safety with superintelligence, but does not identify aligning the first actual superintelligent AI as a goal AI companies should pursue.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention caring for sentient life as a desired property of the first superintelligent AI.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s good to have different approaches. There’s a lot of uncertainty about what will actually be required to make superintelligence safe. So if different groups pursue different ideas, that seems healthy.

With SSI, the idea is to have a very direct focus on safe superintelligence. That gives us the opportunity to pursue a different path, without needing every intermediate step to be a product. Other companies have different constraints, and also different advantages.

Ultimately, though, having a distinctive approach isn’t enough. You need to do the research and discover whether your ideas work. That’s what we’re focused on.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s good to have different approaches. There is a lot that we don’t know about superintelligence, and when there is uncertainty, having several teams pursue different ideas is valuable.

For us, the idea is to focus directly on safe superintelligence. That means organizing the research and the company around that one goal, without having to make each intermediate step into a product. We think that gives us room to pursue a different research path.

Other companies will have their own approaches, and we’ll see what works. I wouldn’t claim that we already know how all of this will fit together. The important question is whether we can make the technical progress that makes safety possible as capabilities advance. That’s what we’re focused on.
